**Karl Maron** (1903–1975) was a German politician, who served as the interior minister of East Germany. He also assumed different posts in East Germany's government.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Maron was born in Berlin on 27 April 1903 and was educated in Russia.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-tblade-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-2)

## Early life and education
Maron was a metal worker.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) In 1926, he joined the Communist Party of Germany (KPD).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) During the Nazi regime, he left Germany in 1934 for Denmark and then settled in Russia.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-tblade-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) He returned to Berlin under the protection of a Russian general a few days after the Red Army captured the city in 1945.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-tblade-1) Following his return he became deputy lord mayor of Berlin and the chief of police.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-maoz-5) As a deputy mayor one of his significant tasks was to rename the streets of Berlin.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-maoz-5) In 1946, he joined the Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-6) From 1946 to 1950 he was the chief editor of daily _Neues Deutschland_, which was founded in 1946 by the SED.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) He was also the director of Berlin municipality's economy department at the end of the 1940s.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-7)

## Early life and education
He became the chief of the German people's police or more commonly Volkspolizei in June 1950 when former chief Kurt Fischer died.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-bes2003-8) In February 1953, he publicly argued "the Volkspolizei can never be neutral or unpolitical."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-bes2003-8) In 1954, he was named as the member of SED's central committee.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) During his tenure as the chief of Volkspolizei he also assumed the role of deputy interior minister.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-9)

## Early life and education
Maron was appointed interior minister on 1 July 1955, replacing Willi Stoph in the post.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-10) In this position he was promoted in 1962 to Generaloberst. In 1961, he became a member of the working group formed by the Politburo to develop ways to end refugee flow from East Germany.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Harrison2011-11) The other members of the group were then security chief Erich Honecker and Stasi chief Erich Mielke.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Harrison2011-11) Maron's tenure as interior minister ended on 14 November 1963.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-cate-12) He was succeeded by Friedrich Dickel as interior minister.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-13) From 1958 to 1967 he served as the representative of Volkskammer.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) In 1964, Maron founded the Institute for Demoscopy (_Institut für Meinungsforschung_ in German) that was a demoscopic research body sponsored by the SED.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-14)

## Personal life and death
[edit]
Maron was the step-father of author Monika Maron.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-cate-12)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-15) Karl Maron married her mother in 1955.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-16) He died in 1975.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-17)
A street in East Berlin was named after him, Karl-Maron-Straße, in the 1970s and 1980s.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-18)

Described by _Le Monde_ as "one of the best writers of her generation," Monika Maron is popularly regarded as the most important GDR author alongside Christa Wolf (1929-2011).

# Monika Maron: Chronicler of the GDR turns 80
But unlike the highly decorated Wolf, Maron did not achieve her writing success in East Germany, where she lived from 1951 to 1988 after she was born and first raised in West Berlin.
Her debut novel _Flight of Ashes_ (1981), the GDR's first "environmental novel," was typically banned in her home country. Drawing on her experience as an industrial reporter, Maron exposed devastating pollution caused by the open cut brown coal mines in the East German town of Bitterfeld, which she called "the dirtiest city in Europe."
When _Flight of Ashes_ was published in West Germany, Maron was 40 years old and remained a struggling writer. It was not until 2009 that she received one of the top awards in her homeland, the German National Prize.

# Monika Maron: Chronicler of the GDR turns 80
## Evolution as a writer in the GDR
Monika Maron had taken up the pen in the mid-1970s after working as a director's assistant, studying theater and art history, and then shifting to journalism.
In her early novels written in East Berlin, her primary theme was life and loathing inside a totalitarian surveillance state.
But despite Maron's criticism of the GDR regime, it turned out that she had worked as an informer for the Ministry of State Security, or Stasi — a fact that she addressed in her 1999 novel, _Pawels Briefe_(Pawel's Letters).
Her connection with the Stasi allegedly allowed her to travel to West Berlin to research her first novel, even if that book would describe censorship and corrupt state industry practices and later be banned.
Maron's ties to the regime began when her mother Hella Iglarz — who had been unable to marry since the Nazi race laws defined her as "half-Jewish" — met Karl Maron, a communist party functionary and later GDR Minister of the Interior. Hella and her daughter moved from West to East Berlin in 1951 before she was married in 1955, with Monika taking her stepfather's name.
So it was not a total surprise when from October 1976, Maron temporarily became an informer. But it would not be long before she herself was put under surveillance for incendiary writings — including the banned 1986 novel, _The Defector_, a feminist tale of individual alienation in the GDR.
By 1988, the East German regime facilitated her exit from the country by granting the writer a three-year visa— an indirect method of expatriation. She moved to Hamburg before returning to West Berlin in 1992.

# Monika Maron: Chronicler of the GDR turns 80
## Chronicling unified Germany
After the fall of the Berlin Wall, Maron became a chronicler of everyday life throughout Germany. At first, she was particularly hard on East Germans who she portrayed as feeling victimized by the West,and unwilling to recognize how broken their country was.

# Monika Maron: Chronicler of the GDR turns 80
## Compelling attempts to escape the GDR
### Across the Baltic in a dinghy
Not everyone in the former East Germany waited until the Wall came down to go west. In 1977, a truck driver from Dresden daringly set out with his wife and daughter in a tiny rubber boat across the Baltic Sea. Fifteen hours later, a fisherman took them on board his trawler and brought them safely to Lübeck in the West. It should be noted, however, that many others died trying to flee by sea.
Image: picture-alliance/dpa/W. Baum

# Monika Maron: Chronicler of the GDR turns 80
## Compelling attempts to escape the GDR
### The other shore
In 1974, biologist Carmen Rohrbach swam out from the GDR into the Baltic with her boyfriend, a rubber boat in tow. Before they could make it to Denmark, a search light went on. They released the boat and continued swimming. Captured by East German guards, Rohrbach then spent two years in prison. Today, she's still an adventurer, traveling far and wide for her research and book-writing.
Image: picture-alliance/dpa/C. Rohrbach

# Monika Maron: Chronicler of the GDR turns 80
## Compelling attempts to escape the GDR
### Swimming to freedom
Axel Mitbauer, a GDR national swim team member, used pure muscle to flee. In 1969, the 19-year-old swam across the Baltic Sea from Boltenhagen to Lübeck's bay area when guards turned search lights off to allow them to cool. "I had one minute to cross both the first and second sandbanks," he recalled. He smeared himself with masses of petroleum jelly to protect himself against the icy temperatures.

**Karl Maron** (IPA: /maʁoːn/) (* 27. April1903 in Charlottenburg; † 2. Februar1975 in Ost-Berlin) war ein deutscher Politiker (KPD, SED). Er war von 1955 bis 1963 Minister des Innern der Deutschen Demokratischen Republik (DDR) und ab 1954 Mitglied des Zentralkomitees der SED.
Der Sohn eines Kutschers absolvierte nach dem Besuch der Volksschule von 1917 bis 1921 eine Ausbildung zum Maschinenschlosser und arbeitete bis 1929 im erlernten Beruf. Seit 1919 war er als Ringer in der Arbeitersportbewegung aktiv. 1926 trat er der Kommunistischen Partei Deutschlands (KPD) bei. Von 1927 bis 1928 war er Mitglied der KPD-Leitung der Siemens-Werke Berlin, seit 1931 Mitglied der Reichsleitung der Kampfgemeinschaft für Rote Sporteinheit und seit 1932 Vorsitzender des Arbeiter-Turn- und Sportvereins „Fichte“.
In der Folge der Machtergreifung der Nationalsozialisten 1933 war Maron illegal tätig und emigrierte 1934 nach Kopenhagen, wo er Redakteur des Pressedienstes der Roten Sportinternationale (RSI) wurde.
Seit 1935 war er Vertreter der RSI beim Exekutivkomitee der Kommunistischen Internationale (EKKI) in Moskau und nach Auflösung der RSI 1937 Mitarbeiter der Presse- und Informationsabteilung des EKKI. Während des Zweiten Weltkrieges war er von 1943 bis 1945 Redakteur der Zeitung _Freies Deutschland_ des Nationalkomitees Freies Deutschland und dabei verantwortlich für die Kriegsberichterstattung.
Im Jahr 1945 kehrte er mit der Gruppe Ackermann in Folge der „Gruppe Ulbricht“ nach Deutschland zurück. Bis 1946 war er 1. Stellvertreter des Oberbürgermeisters von Berlin im Magistrat Werner.

Mit der Zwangsvereinigung von SPD und KPD wurde er Mitglied der Sozialistischen Einheitspartei Deutschlands (SED), war bis 1949 SED-Stadtverordneter und ab 1948 Stadtrat für Wirtschaft im sowjetischen Sektor Berlins. 1948 nahm Maron an den Verhandlungen über eine gemeinsame Verfassung von Berlin teil.
Von 1949 bis 1950 war er stellvertretender Chefredakteur des SED-Zentralorgans_Neues Deutschland_.
Grabstätte in der _Gedenkstätte der Sozialisten_
1950 wurde Maron im Range eines Generalinspekteurs als Nachfolger des verstorbenen Kurt Fischer Chef der Deutschen Volkspolizei und stellvertretender Innenminister. Maron war seit 1954 Mitglied des Zentralkomitees (ZK) der SED und von 1958 bis 1967 Abgeordneter der Volkskammer. Von 1955 bis 1963 war er als Nachfolger von Willi StophMinister des Innern und gleichzeitig Chef der Deutschen Volkspolizei, zuletzt seit 1962 im Range eines Generalobersten. 1961 war er Mitglied des Stabes des Nationalen Verteidigungsrats und damit auch am Bau der Berliner Mauer beteiligt.
1963 trat Maron aus gesundheitlichen Gründen als Minister des Innern und Chef der Deutschen Volkspolizei zurück. Ab 1964 war er Leiter des Institutes für Meinungsforschung beim ZK der SED.
Seine Urne ist in der Gedenkstätte der Sozialisten auf dem Zentralfriedhof Friedrichsfelde in Berlin-Lichtenberg beigesetzt.

Karl Maron war seit 1955 mit Hella, geborene Iglarz (1915–2010), verheiratet und damit Stiefvater der Schriftstellerin Monika Maron. **Karl Maron** (1903–1975) was a German politician, who served as the interior minister of East Germany. He also assumed different posts in East Germany's government.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Maron was born in Berlin on 27 April 1903 and was educated in Russia.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-tblade-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-2)
texts.2:
## Early life and education
Maron was a metal worker.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) In 1926, he joined the Communist Party of Germany (KPD).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) During the Nazi regime, he left Germany in 1934 for Denmark and then settled in Russia.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-tblade-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) He returned to Berlin under the protection of a Russian general a few days after the Red Army captured the city in 1945.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-tblade-1) Following his return he became deputy lord mayor of Berlin and the chief of police.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-maoz-5) As a deputy mayor one of his significant tasks was to rename the streets of Berlin.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-maoz-5) In 1946, he joined the Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-6) From 1946 to 1950 he was the chief editor of daily _Neues Deutschland_, which was founded in 1946 by the SED.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) He was also the director of Berlin municipality's economy department at the end of the 1940s.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-7)
texts.3:
## Early life and education
He became the chief of the German people's police or more commonly Volkspolizei in June 1950 when former chief Kurt Fischer died.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-bes2003-8) In February 1953, he publicly argued "the Volkspolizei can never be neutral or unpolitical."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-bes2003-8) In 1954, he was named as the member of SED's central committee.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) During his tenure as the chief of Volkspolizei he also assumed the role of deputy interior minister.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-9)
texts.4:
## Early life and education
Maron was appointed interior minister on 1 July 1955, replacing Willi Stoph in the post.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-10) In this position he was promoted in 1962 to Generaloberst. In 1961, he became a member of the working group formed by the Politburo to develop ways to end refugee flow from East Germany.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Harrison2011-11) The other members of the group were then security chief Erich Honecker and Stasi chief Erich Mielke.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Harrison2011-11) Maron's tenure as interior minister ended on 14 November 1963.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-cate-12) He was succeeded by Friedrich Dickel as interior minister.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-13) From 1958 to 1967 he served as the representative of Volkskammer.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) In 1964, Maron founded the Institute for Demoscopy (_Institut für Meinungsforschung_ in German) that was a demoscopic research body sponsored by the SED.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-14)

## Personal life and death
[edit]
Maron was the step-father of author Monika Maron.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-cate-12)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-15) Karl Maron married her mother in 1955.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-16) He died in 1975.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-17)
A street in East Berlin was named after him, Karl-Maron-Straße, in the 1970s and 1980s.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-18)

**Karl Maron** (IPA: /maʁoːn/) (* 27. April1903 in Charlottenburg; † 2. Februar1975 in Ost-Berlin) war ein deutscher Politiker (KPD, SED). Er war von 1955 bis 1963 Minister des Innern der Deutschen Demokratischen Republik (DDR) und ab 1954 Mitglied des Zentralkomitees der SED.
Der Sohn eines Kutschers absolvierte nach dem Besuch der Volksschule von 1917 bis 1921 eine Ausbildung zum Maschinenschlosser und arbeitete bis 1929 im erlernten Beruf. Seit 1919 war er als Ringer in der Arbeitersportbewegung aktiv. 1926 trat er der Kommunistischen Partei Deutschlands (KPD) bei. Von 1927 bis 1928 war er Mitglied der KPD-Leitung der Siemens-Werke Berlin, seit 1931 Mitglied der Reichsleitung der Kampfgemeinschaft für Rote Sporteinheit und seit 1932 Vorsitzender des Arbeiter-Turn- und Sportvereins „Fichte“.
In der Folge der Machtergreifung der Nationalsozialisten 1933 war Maron illegal tätig und emigrierte 1934 nach Kopenhagen, wo er Redakteur des Pressedienstes der Roten Sportinternationale (RSI) wurde.
Seit 1935 war er Vertreter der RSI beim Exekutivkomitee der Kommunistischen Internationale (EKKI) in Moskau und nach Auflösung der RSI 1937 Mitarbeiter der Presse- und Informationsabteilung des EKKI. Während des Zweiten Weltkrieges war er von 1943 bis 1945 Redakteur der Zeitung _Freies Deutschland_ des Nationalkomitees Freies Deutschland und dabei verantwortlich für die Kriegsberichterstattung.
Im Jahr 1945 kehrte er mit der Gruppe Ackermann in Folge der „Gruppe Ulbricht“ nach Deutschland zurück. Bis 1946 war er 1. Stellvertreter des Oberbürgermeisters von Berlin im Magistrat Werner.

Von 1949 bis 1950 war er stellvertretender Chefredakteur des SED-Zentralorgans_Neues Deutschland_.

1950 wurde Maron im Range eines Generalinspekteurs als Nachfolger des verstorbenen Kurt Fischer Chef der Deutschen Volkspolizei und stellvertretender Innenminister. Maron war seit 1954 Mitglied des Zentralkomitees (ZK) der SED und von 1958 bis 1967 Abgeordneter der Volkskammer. Von 1955 bis 1963 war er als Nachfolger von Willi StophMinister des Innern und gleichzeitig Chef der Deutschen Volkspolizei, zuletzt seit 1962 im Range eines Generalobersten. 1961 war er Mitglied des Stabes des Nationalen Verteidigungsrats und damit auch am Bau der Berliner Mauer beteiligt.
1963 trat Maron aus gesundheitlichen Gründen als Minister des Innern und Chef der Deutschen Volkspolizei zurück. Ab 1964 war er Leiter des Institutes für Meinungsforschung beim ZK der SED.
Seine Urne ist in der Gedenkstätte der Sozialisten auf dem Zentralfriedhof Friedrichsfelde in Berlin-Lichtenberg beigesetzt.

# Monika Maron: Chronicler of the GDR turns 80
But unlike the highly decorated Wolf, Maron did not achieve her writing success in East Germany, where she lived from 1951 to 1988 after she was born and first raised in West Berlin.
Her debut novel _Flight of Ashes_ (1981), the GDR's first "environmental novel," was typically banned in her home country. Drawing on her experience as an industrial reporter, Maron exposed devastating pollution caused by the open cut brown coal mines in the East German town of Bitterfeld, which she called "the dirtiest city in Europe."
When _Flight of Ashes_ was published in West Germany, Maron was 40 years old and remained a struggling writer. It was not until 2009 that she received one of the top awards in her homeland, the German National Prize.

# Monika Maron: Chronicler of the GDR turns 80
## Evolution as a writer in the GDR
Monika Maron had taken up the pen in the mid-1970s after working as a director's assistant, studying theater and art history, and then shifting to journalism.
In her early novels written in East Berlin, her primary theme was life and loathing inside a totalitarian surveillance state.
But despite Maron's criticism of the GDR regime, it turned out that she had worked as an informer for the Ministry of State Security, or Stasi — a fact that she addressed in her 1999 novel, _Pawels Briefe_(Pawel's Letters).
Her connection with the Stasi allegedly allowed her to travel to West Berlin to research her first novel, even if that book would describe censorship and corrupt state industry practices and later be banned.
Maron's ties to the regime began when her mother Hella Iglarz — who had been unable to marry since the Nazi race laws defined her as "half-Jewish" — met Karl Maron, a communist party functionary and later GDR Minister of the Interior. Hella and her daughter moved from West to East Berlin in 1951 before she was married in 1955, with Monika taking her stepfather's name.
So it was not a total surprise when from October 1976, Maron temporarily became an informer. But it would not be long before she herself was put under surveillance for incendiary writings — including the banned 1986 novel, _The Defector_, a feminist tale of individual alienation in the GDR.
By 1988, the East German regime facilitated her exit from the country by granting the writer a three-year visa— an indirect method of expatriation. She moved to Hamburg before returning to West Berlin in 1992.

**Karl Maron** (1903–1975) was a German politician, who served as the interior minister of East Germany. He also assumed different posts in East Germany's government.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Maron was born in Berlin on 27 April 1903 and was educated in Russia.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-tblade-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-2)

## Early life and education
Maron was a metal worker.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) In 1926, he joined the Communist Party of Germany (KPD).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) During the Nazi regime, he left Germany in 1934 for Denmark and then settled in Russia.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-tblade-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) He returned to Berlin under the protection of a Russian general a few days after the Red Army captured the city in 1945.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-tblade-1) Following his return he became deputy lord mayor of Berlin and the chief of police.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-maoz-5) As a deputy mayor one of his significant tasks was to rename the streets of Berlin.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-maoz-5) In 1946, he joined the Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-6) From 1946 to 1950 he was the chief editor of daily _Neues Deutschland_, which was founded in 1946 by the SED.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) He was also the director of Berlin municipality's economy department at the end of the 1940s.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-7)

## Early life and education
He became the chief of the German people's police or more commonly Volkspolizei in June 1950 when former chief Kurt Fischer died.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-bes2003-8) In February 1953, he publicly argued "the Volkspolizei can never be neutral or unpolitical."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-bes2003-8) In 1954, he was named as the member of SED's central committee.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) During his tenure as the chief of Volkspolizei he also assumed the role of deputy interior minister.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-9)

## Early life and education
Maron was appointed interior minister on 1 July 1955, replacing Willi Stoph in the post.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-10) In this position he was promoted in 1962 to Generaloberst. In 1961, he became a member of the working group formed by the Politburo to develop ways to end refugee flow from East Germany.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Harrison2011-11) The other members of the group were then security chief Erich Honecker and Stasi chief Erich Mielke.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Harrison2011-11) Maron's tenure as interior minister ended on 14 November 1963.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-cate-12) He was succeeded by Friedrich Dickel as interior minister.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-13) From 1958 to 1967 he served as the representative of Volkskammer.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3) In 1964, Maron founded the Institute for Demoscopy (_Institut für Meinungsforschung_ in German) that was a demoscopic research body sponsored by the SED.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-14)

## Personal life and death
[edit]
Maron was the step-father of author Monika Maron.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-cate-12)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-15) Karl Maron married her mother in 1955.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-16) He died in 1975.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-Schaumann2008-3)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-17)
A street in East Berlin was named after him, Karl-Maron-Straße, in the 1970s and 1980s.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Maron#cite_note-18)

## Evolution as a writer in the GDR
Monika Maron had taken up the pen in the mid-1970s after working as a director's assistant, studying theater and art history, and then shifting to journalism.
In her early novels written in East Berlin, her primary theme was life and loathing inside a totalitarian surveillance state.
But despite Maron's criticism of the GDR regime, it turned out that she had worked as an informer for the Ministry of State Security, or Stasi — a fact that she addressed in her 1999 novel, _Pawels Briefe_(Pawel's Letters).
Her connection with the Stasi allegedly allowed her to travel to West Berlin to research her first novel, even if that book would describe censorship and corrupt state industry practices and later be banned.
Maron's ties to the regime began when her mother Hella Iglarz — who had been unable to marry since the Nazi race laws defined her as "half-Jewish" — met Karl Maron, a communist party functionary and later GDR Minister of the Interior. Hella and her daughter moved from West to East Berlin in 1951 before she was married in 1955, with Monika taking her stepfather's name.
So it was not a total surprise when from October 1976, Maron temporarily became an informer. But it would not be long before she herself was put under surveillance for incendiary writings — including the banned 1986 novel, _The Defector_, a feminist tale of individual alienation in the GDR.
By 1988, the East German regime facilitated her exit from the country by granting the writer a three-year visa— an indirect method of expatriation. She moved to Hamburg before returning to West Berlin in 1992.

The **Border Troops of the German Democratic Republic** (German: _Grenztruppen der DDR_) was the border guard of the German Democratic Republic (GDR) from 1946 to 1990.
The _Grenztruppen_ were the primary force guarding the Berlin Wall and the Inner German border, the GDR's international borders between West Berlin and West Germany respectively. The force belonged to the Ministry of National Defence (MfNV) from 1961, and was a service branch of the [National People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Army "National People's Army") until 1971 when it became directly subordinate to the MfNV. The Border Troops numbered approximately 47,000 personnel at its peak, consisting of volunteers and conscripts, the third-largest Warsaw Pact border guard after the Soviet Border Troops and Poland's Border Protection Troops.
The _Grenztruppen_'s main role was preventing _Republikflucht_, the illegal migration from the GDR, and were controversially responsible for many deaths at the Berlin Wall.

An East German _Grenzaufklärungszug_ (GAK) border trooper taking pictures of US Army activities across the inner German border
_Grenztruppen_ guarding maintenance workers on the western side of the inner German border fence. The red tape in the foreground, the so-called "death cord", marked the area the work detail was permitted to operate, and workers stepping beyond the tape would be shot
_Grenztruppen_ during an exercise near Mühlhausen on March 27, 1982
By December 1945, within six months of the end of the Second World War, each of the five states in the Soviet Zone of Occupation had new police forces in clear violation of the Yalta and Potsdam agreements_[citation needed_]. In early January 1946, the name _Volkspolizei_ (People's Police) was publicly applied to the new police forces in the Soviet Zone, and in August these forces were placed under the centralized control of the newly created German Administration of the Interior, headed by Erich Reschke. On 1 December 1946, the _Deutsche Grenzpolizei_ (German Border Police) was organized by the Soviet Military Administration in Germany (SMAD) as a paramilitary to defend the borders of the Soviet Zone. The initial 3,000 recruits of the _Grenzpolizei_ were organized and trained from _Volkspolizei_ resources, and by April 1948 numbered 10,000 personnel before rising to 18,000 in 1950. The _Grenzpolizei_ were armed and organized like a police force, and were subordinate to the Main Administration of the Border Police and Alert Units of the German Administration of the Interior. The Soviet Zone was formed into the German Democratic Republic (GDR or East Germany) in October 1949 and led by the Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED) under Soviet influence. The SED reorganized the _Grenzpolizei_ along military lines, similar to the USSR's Border Troops, and briefly transferred them from the Ministry of the Interior (_Ministerium des Innern_) to the Ministry of State Security (MfS or _Stasi_) from May 1952 to June 1953.
East German border guard Konrad Schumann fleeing East Germany, 1961

In 1961, the _Grenzpolizei_ were reorganized as the Border Troops of the GDR (_Grenztruppen der DDR_) and were moved from the Ministry of the Interior, which oversaw policing, to the Ministry of National Defence (MfNV) which oversaw the military. The _Grenztruppen_ became the fourth service branch of the [National People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Army "National People's Army") (NVA), the armed forces of the GDR. In 1973 they were separated and became directly subordinate to the MfNV, on grounds of not to be counted in MBFR. While wearing standard NVA uniforms, the _Grenztruppen_ had their own dark green arm-of-service colour, and their service and dress uniforms bore a green cuff title with white lettering "_Grenztruppen der DDR_" on the left arm. The vast majority of _Grenztruppen_ efforts were directed along the GDR's western borders with West Germany and West Berlin, with only about 600 members assigned to guard the GDR's borders with [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Poland "People's Republic of Poland") and Czechoslovakia. This continued until the 1980s when the rise of the Solidarity trade union in Poland saw the GDR considerably toughen the _Grenztruppen_'s presence along their border.
On 1 July 1990, the GDR's border control regime along the borders with West Germany and West Berlin was ended. In September 1990, shortly before the reunification of Germany, the _Grenztruppen_ were disbanded; its border patrol duties along united Germany's eastern frontiers were assumed by the _Bundesgrenzschutz_ (Federal Border Guard – later the _Bundespolizei_ or Federal Police).

## Pass and control units
[edit]
West German border personnel, civilians and an East German border guard on opposite sides of the border line at Herrnburg near Lübeck
For most visitors to East Berlin and the GDR, including persons who utilized the land transit routes (road and rail) between West Germany and West Berlin, their exposure to the _Grenztruppen der DDR_ consisted of dealing with the members of the Pass and Control Units (_Paß- und Kontrolleinheiten_, PKE) who processed travelers passing through the GDR's _Grenzübergangsstellen_ (border crossing points). Although they wore _Grenztruppen_ uniforms, the members of the PKE were in fact members of the 6th Main Department _(Hauptabteilung VI)_ of the _Stasi_.

## Organizational structure
[edit]
The headquarters of the _Grenztruppen der DDR_ was located at Bestensee-Pätz (a small village southeast of Berlin in the present-day state of Brandenburg), near Königs Wusterhausen.
The **_Grenzkommando Nord_** (GKN) [Border Command North], with headquarters at Stendal (in the present-day state of Saxony-Anhalt) was responsible for the northern sector of the East German border. The GKN consisted of five frontier troops regiments, two training regiments, a helicopter flight and some smaller support units. The _Grenzregiment 25 "Neithardt von Gneisenau"_ was disbanded in August 1983 and its units dispersed among the other border regiments of the command.
The **_Grenzkommando Süd_** (GKS) [Border Command South], with headquarters at Erfurt, guarded the southern border sector. The organizational structure of the GKS was similar to that of the GKN, with six frontier troops regiments, two training regiments, a helicopter flight and some smaller support units.

## After the Wall: The End of the Grenztruppen
The border troops did not survive the state they had defended. On 21 September 1990, ten days before German reunification, Defence Minister Rainer Eppelmann signed _Befehl_ 49/90, formally dissolving the _Grenztruppen der DDR_. Responsibility for the border passed to the _Bundesgrenzschutz_ (Federal Border Guard). Some former border soldiers were absorbed into the new structures; many were dismissed.
The border itself took years to remove. Under Bundeswehr direction, teams, some of them former border troops who knew the installations better than anyone, cleared the mines, dismantled the fences and watchtowers, tore up the patrol roads, and filled in the anti-vehicle ditches. The work continued until 1994. Today the death strip has become the _Berliner Mauerweg_, a 160-kilometre walking and cycling path that traces the entire circuit of the former Wall through the city. Where guards once patrolled with orders to kill, joggers and cyclists pass without a thought.

## The Watchtowers You Can Visit Today
Five watchtowers from the Berlin Wall fortifications survive in and around the city. Each has a different character, and together they give a physical sense of what the border looked like from the inside: the cramped observation rooms, the narrow stairs, the view across the death strip that the guards saw every shift.
The Grenzturm Nieder Neuendorf, a preserved command tower on the Havel, now a museum documenting the daily reality of the border service
The Gedenkstätte Günter Litfin in the Kieler Eck command tower near Berlin Hauptbahnhof is the most personal of the five. It was established and run for years by Jürgen Litfin, the brother of Günter Litfin, the first person shot dead at the Berlin Wall on 24 August 1961. The tower preserves the observation room and tells both Günter’s story and the broader history of the border fortifications at this stretch of the Spree.
The Führungsstelle Schlesischer Busch stands in Kreuzberg, on the edge of the former death strip near the Landwehr Canal. This was a command post rather than a simple observation tower, coordinating patrols across the sector. It now hosts a small exhibition on the border regime and temporary art shows.
The Wachturm Erna-Berger-Straße, just south of Potsdamer Platz, is a round observation tower of the BT-11 type that was standard along the Berlin Wall. Surrounded today by government buildings and new construction, it is a startling survivor — a piece of the fortified border standing in the middle of the reunified capital.
Further out, the Grenzturm Nieder Neuendorf sits on the bank of the Havel river northwest of Berlin. This is the most complete of the five: a full command tower with a well-preserved interior, now a museum that documents the daily reality of the border service: shift rosters, observation logs, the view the guards actually had. It is the closest thing to standing inside the system.
The Bergfelde Watchtower, in Brandenburg just beyond the Berlin city line, marks the outer ring of the fortifications. It stands at the edge of open fields where the border ran through farmland rather than city streets, a reminder that the Wall was only the urban face of a much longer frontier.

## Frequently Asked Questions
Günter Litfin tower memorial stone © André Karwath aka Aka

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Did the border guards really have a shoot-to-kill order?
Yes. The _Schießbefehl_ was not a single document but a chain of written orders and oral instructions from 1961 to 1989, each authorizing lethal force against border crossers. Guards were trained to hit with the first shot, rewarded for killing, and punished for failing to fire. The order was secretly lifted on 3 April 1989, seven weeks after the last fatal shooting. See the full timeline above.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many people did the border guards kill?
At least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall between 1961 and 1989, the majority shot by border guards. On the whole inner-German border (from the Baltic coast to the Czech frontier) the total is higher. Eight border guards themselves were also killed on duty at the Berlin Wall.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many border guards escaped to the West?
About 2,500 border troops successfully defected over the life of the Wall, out of roughly 7,000 who attempted it. The most famous was Conrad Schumann, who jumped over the barbed wire on Bernauer Straße on 15 August 1961. Around 5,500 who tried and failed were caught and imprisoned.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Were the border guards punished after reunification?
Yes. In the _Mauerschuetzenprozesse_ (border-shooter trials) that ran through the 1990s, Berlin courts convicted 132 people: 80 guards, 42 military commanders, and 10 SED political leaders including Egon Krenz. The European Court of Human Rights upheld the convictions in 2001, ruling that the law of the GDR could not shield those who killed unarmed people trying to leave the country.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Can you visit a Berlin Wall watchtower today?
Yes. Five watchtowers survive in and around Berlin, all marked on the interactive map. The Grenzturm Nieder Neuendorf has the most complete museum interior, while the Gedenkstätte Günter Litfin near Hauptbahnhof is the most central. See the watchtowers section above for all five.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many Berlin Wall watchtowers are left?
Five survive: the Gedenkstätte Günter Litfin (Kieler Eck), the Führungsstelle Schlesischer Busch, the Wachturm Erna-Berger-Straße, the Grenzturm Nieder Neuendorf, and the Bergfelde Watchtower. At the Wall’s peak, there were more than 300 watchtowers along the border around West Berlin alone.
Find all five watchtowers and every other site of the divided city on our interactive Berlin Wall map, or follow the full arc from the barbed wire to the fall on the Berlin Wall history timeline.

The patch on his sleeve reads “Grenztruppen,” the Border Troops of the German Democratic Republic. Their main job wasn’t keeping enemies out. It was keeping East Germans from leaving.
After millions of people fled to the West in the 1950s, East Germany sealed its borders. The Berlin Wall went up in August 1961, and the nearly 870-mile border between East and West Germany was lined with fences, minefields, watchtowers and patrol strips.
A year later, East Germany introduced compulsory military service. Young men were drafted at 18 for 18 months, and many were assigned to the border. Most of the rank and file were conscripts led by career officers.
Guards were under orders to stop escapes by any means, including deadly force. At least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall alone, and hundreds more along the wider border. Some of those trying to escape were the same age as the guards ordered to stop them.
Not every member of the Border Troops stood on the line with a rifle. Many worked in offices, communications and planning, like the young man in this photo, marking up a chart at a desk.
When the Wall fell in November 1989, the Border Troops lost their purpose almost overnight. They were disbanded in 1990.
Added fact: One of the most famous photos of the Cold War shows an East German border guard escaping. In August 1961, 19-year-old Conrad Schumann leaped over the barbed wire in Berlin to freedom in the West, just days after the border was sealed.

The **Border Troops of the German Democratic Republic** (German: _Grenztruppen der DDR_) was the border guard of the German Democratic Republic (GDR) from 1946 to 1990.
The _Grenztruppen_ were the primary force guarding the Berlin Wall and the Inner German border, the GDR's international borders between West Berlin and West Germany respectively. The force belonged to the Ministry of National Defence (MfNV) from 1961, and was a service branch of the [National People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Army "National People's Army") until 1971 when it became directly subordinate to the MfNV. The Border Troops numbered approximately 47,000 personnel at its peak, consisting of volunteers and conscripts, the third-largest Warsaw Pact border guard after the Soviet Border Troops and Poland's Border Protection Troops.
The _Grenztruppen_'s main role was preventing _Republikflucht_, the illegal migration from the GDR, and were controversially responsible for many deaths at the Berlin Wall.

An East German _Grenzaufklärungszug_ (GAK) border trooper taking pictures of US Army activities across the inner German border
_Grenztruppen_ guarding maintenance workers on the western side of the inner German border fence. The red tape in the foreground, the so-called "death cord", marked the area the work detail was permitted to operate, and workers stepping beyond the tape would be shot
_Grenztruppen_ during an exercise near Mühlhausen on March 27, 1982
By December 1945, within six months of the end of the Second World War, each of the five states in the Soviet Zone of Occupation had new police forces in clear violation of the Yalta and Potsdam agreements_[citation needed_]. In early January 1946, the name _Volkspolizei_ (People's Police) was publicly applied to the new police forces in the Soviet Zone, and in August these forces were placed under the centralized control of the newly created German Administration of the Interior, headed by Erich Reschke. On 1 December 1946, the _Deutsche Grenzpolizei_ (German Border Police) was organized by the Soviet Military Administration in Germany (SMAD) as a paramilitary to defend the borders of the Soviet Zone. The initial 3,000 recruits of the _Grenzpolizei_ were organized and trained from _Volkspolizei_ resources, and by April 1948 numbered 10,000 personnel before rising to 18,000 in 1950. The _Grenzpolizei_ were armed and organized like a police force, and were subordinate to the Main Administration of the Border Police and Alert Units of the German Administration of the Interior. The Soviet Zone was formed into the German Democratic Republic (GDR or East Germany) in October 1949 and led by the Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED) under Soviet influence. The SED reorganized the _Grenzpolizei_ along military lines, similar to the USSR's Border Troops, and briefly transferred them from the Ministry of the Interior (_Ministerium des Innern_) to the Ministry of State Security (MfS or _Stasi_) from May 1952 to June 1953.
East German border guard Konrad Schumann fleeing East Germany, 1961
texts.2:
In 1961, the _Grenzpolizei_ were reorganized as the Border Troops of the GDR (_Grenztruppen der DDR_) and were moved from the Ministry of the Interior, which oversaw policing, to the Ministry of National Defence (MfNV) which oversaw the military. The _Grenztruppen_ became the fourth service branch of the [National People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Army "National People's Army") (NVA), the armed forces of the GDR. In 1973 they were separated and became directly subordinate to the MfNV, on grounds of not to be counted in MBFR. While wearing standard NVA uniforms, the _Grenztruppen_ had their own dark green arm-of-service colour, and their service and dress uniforms bore a green cuff title with white lettering "_Grenztruppen der DDR_" on the left arm. The vast majority of _Grenztruppen_ efforts were directed along the GDR's western borders with West Germany and West Berlin, with only about 600 members assigned to guard the GDR's borders with [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Poland "People's Republic of Poland") and Czechoslovakia. This continued until the 1980s when the rise of the Solidarity trade union in Poland saw the GDR considerably toughen the _Grenztruppen_'s presence along their border.
On 1 July 1990, the GDR's border control regime along the borders with West Germany and West Berlin was ended. In September 1990, shortly before the reunification of Germany, the _Grenztruppen_ were disbanded; its border patrol duties along united Germany's eastern frontiers were assumed by the _Bundesgrenzschutz_ (Federal Border Guard – later the _Bundespolizei_ or Federal Police).
texts.3:
## Pass and control units
[edit]
West German border personnel, civilians and an East German border guard on opposite sides of the border line at Herrnburg near Lübeck
For most visitors to East Berlin and the GDR, including persons who utilized the land transit routes (road and rail) between West Germany and West Berlin, their exposure to the _Grenztruppen der DDR_ consisted of dealing with the members of the Pass and Control Units (_Paß- und Kontrolleinheiten_, PKE) who processed travelers passing through the GDR's _Grenzübergangsstellen_ (border crossing points). Although they wore _Grenztruppen_ uniforms, the members of the PKE were in fact members of the 6th Main Department _(Hauptabteilung VI)_ of the _Stasi_.
texts.4:
## Organizational structure
[edit]
The headquarters of the _Grenztruppen der DDR_ was located at Bestensee-Pätz (a small village southeast of Berlin in the present-day state of Brandenburg), near Königs Wusterhausen.
The **_Grenzkommando Nord_** (GKN) [Border Command North], with headquarters at Stendal (in the present-day state of Saxony-Anhalt) was responsible for the northern sector of the East German border. The GKN consisted of five frontier troops regiments, two training regiments, a helicopter flight and some smaller support units. The _Grenzregiment 25 "Neithardt von Gneisenau"_ was disbanded in August 1983 and its units dispersed among the other border regiments of the command.
The **_Grenzkommando Süd_** (GKS) [Border Command South], with headquarters at Erfurt, guarded the southern border sector. The organizational structure of the GKS was similar to that of the GKN, with six frontier troops regiments, two training regiments, a helicopter flight and some smaller support units.

texts.10:
## After the Wall: The End of the Grenztruppen
The border troops did not survive the state they had defended. On 21 September 1990, ten days before German reunification, Defence Minister Rainer Eppelmann signed _Befehl_ 49/90, formally dissolving the _Grenztruppen der DDR_. Responsibility for the border passed to the _Bundesgrenzschutz_ (Federal Border Guard). Some former border soldiers were absorbed into the new structures; many were dismissed.
The border itself took years to remove. Under Bundeswehr direction, teams, some of them former border troops who knew the installations better than anyone, cleared the mines, dismantled the fences and watchtowers, tore up the patrol roads, and filled in the anti-vehicle ditches. The work continued until 1994. Today the death strip has become the _Berliner Mauerweg_, a 160-kilometre walking and cycling path that traces the entire circuit of the former Wall through the city. Where guards once patrolled with orders to kill, joggers and cyclists pass without a thought.
texts.11:
## The Watchtowers You Can Visit Today
Five watchtowers from the Berlin Wall fortifications survive in and around the city. Each has a different character, and together they give a physical sense of what the border looked like from the inside: the cramped observation rooms, the narrow stairs, the view across the death strip that the guards saw every shift.
The Grenzturm Nieder Neuendorf, a preserved command tower on the Havel, now a museum documenting the daily reality of the border service
The Gedenkstätte Günter Litfin in the Kieler Eck command tower near Berlin Hauptbahnhof is the most personal of the five. It was established and run for years by Jürgen Litfin, the brother of Günter Litfin, the first person shot dead at the Berlin Wall on 24 August 1961. The tower preserves the observation room and tells both Günter’s story and the broader history of the border fortifications at this stretch of the Spree.
The Führungsstelle Schlesischer Busch stands in Kreuzberg, on the edge of the former death strip near the Landwehr Canal. This was a command post rather than a simple observation tower, coordinating patrols across the sector. It now hosts a small exhibition on the border regime and temporary art shows.
The Wachturm Erna-Berger-Straße, just south of Potsdamer Platz, is a round observation tower of the BT-11 type that was standard along the Berlin Wall. Surrounded today by government buildings and new construction, it is a startling survivor — a piece of the fortified border standing in the middle of the reunified capital.
Further out, the Grenzturm Nieder Neuendorf sits on the bank of the Havel river northwest of Berlin. This is the most complete of the five: a full command tower with a well-preserved interior, now a museum that documents the daily reality of the border service: shift rosters, observation logs, the view the guards actually had. It is the closest thing to standing inside the system.
The Bergfelde Watchtower, in Brandenburg just beyond the Berlin city line, marks the outer ring of the fortifications. It stands at the edge of open fields where the border ran through farmland rather than city streets, a reminder that the Wall was only the urban face of a much longer frontier.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Did the border guards really have a shoot-to-kill order?
Yes. The _Schießbefehl_ was not a single document but a chain of written orders and oral instructions from 1961 to 1989, each authorizing lethal force against border crossers. Guards were trained to hit with the first shot, rewarded for killing, and punished for failing to fire. The order was secretly lifted on 3 April 1989, seven weeks after the last fatal shooting. See the full timeline above.
texts.14:
## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many people did the border guards kill?
At least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall between 1961 and 1989, the majority shot by border guards. On the whole inner-German border (from the Baltic coast to the Czech frontier) the total is higher. Eight border guards themselves were also killed on duty at the Berlin Wall.
texts.15:
## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many border guards escaped to the West?
About 2,500 border troops successfully defected over the life of the Wall, out of roughly 7,000 who attempted it. The most famous was Conrad Schumann, who jumped over the barbed wire on Bernauer Straße on 15 August 1961. Around 5,500 who tried and failed were caught and imprisoned.
texts.16:
## Frequently Asked Questions
### Were the border guards punished after reunification?
Yes. In the _Mauerschuetzenprozesse_ (border-shooter trials) that ran through the 1990s, Berlin courts convicted 132 people: 80 guards, 42 military commanders, and 10 SED political leaders including Egon Krenz. The European Court of Human Rights upheld the convictions in 2001, ruling that the law of the GDR could not shield those who killed unarmed people trying to leave the country.
texts.17:
## Frequently Asked Questions
### Can you visit a Berlin Wall watchtower today?
Yes. Five watchtowers survive in and around Berlin, all marked on the interactive map. The Grenzturm Nieder Neuendorf has the most complete museum interior, while the Gedenkstätte Günter Litfin near Hauptbahnhof is the most central. See the watchtowers section above for all five.
texts.18:
## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many Berlin Wall watchtowers are left?
Five survive: the Gedenkstätte Günter Litfin (Kieler Eck), the Führungsstelle Schlesischer Busch, the Wachturm Erna-Berger-Straße, the Grenzturm Nieder Neuendorf, and the Bergfelde Watchtower. At the Wall’s peak, there were more than 300 watchtowers along the border around West Berlin alone.

The **Border Troops of the German Democratic Republic** (German: _Grenztruppen der DDR_) was the border guard of the German Democratic Republic (GDR) from 1946 to 1990.
The _Grenztruppen_ were the primary force guarding the Berlin Wall and the Inner German border, the GDR's international borders between West Berlin and West Germany respectively. The force belonged to the Ministry of National Defence (MfNV) from 1961, and was a service branch of the [National People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Army "National People's Army") until 1971 when it became directly subordinate to the MfNV. The Border Troops numbered approximately 47,000 personnel at its peak, consisting of volunteers and conscripts, the third-largest Warsaw Pact border guard after the Soviet Border Troops and Poland's Border Protection Troops.
The _Grenztruppen_'s main role was preventing _Republikflucht_, the illegal migration from the GDR, and were controversially responsible for many deaths at the Berlin Wall.

An East German _Grenzaufklärungszug_ (GAK) border trooper taking pictures of US Army activities across the inner German border
_Grenztruppen_ guarding maintenance workers on the western side of the inner German border fence. The red tape in the foreground, the so-called "death cord", marked the area the work detail was permitted to operate, and workers stepping beyond the tape would be shot
_Grenztruppen_ during an exercise near Mühlhausen on March 27, 1982
By December 1945, within six months of the end of the Second World War, each of the five states in the Soviet Zone of Occupation had new police forces in clear violation of the Yalta and Potsdam agreements_[citation needed_]. In early January 1946, the name _Volkspolizei_ (People's Police) was publicly applied to the new police forces in the Soviet Zone, and in August these forces were placed under the centralized control of the newly created German Administration of the Interior, headed by Erich Reschke. On 1 December 1946, the _Deutsche Grenzpolizei_ (German Border Police) was organized by the Soviet Military Administration in Germany (SMAD) as a paramilitary to defend the borders of the Soviet Zone. The initial 3,000 recruits of the _Grenzpolizei_ were organized and trained from _Volkspolizei_ resources, and by April 1948 numbered 10,000 personnel before rising to 18,000 in 1950. The _Grenzpolizei_ were armed and organized like a police force, and were subordinate to the Main Administration of the Border Police and Alert Units of the German Administration of the Interior. The Soviet Zone was formed into the German Democratic Republic (GDR or East Germany) in October 1949 and led by the Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED) under Soviet influence. The SED reorganized the _Grenzpolizei_ along military lines, similar to the USSR's Border Troops, and briefly transferred them from the Ministry of the Interior (_Ministerium des Innern_) to the Ministry of State Security (MfS or _Stasi_) from May 1952 to June 1953.
East German border guard Konrad Schumann fleeing East Germany, 1961

In 1961, the _Grenzpolizei_ were reorganized as the Border Troops of the GDR (_Grenztruppen der DDR_) and were moved from the Ministry of the Interior, which oversaw policing, to the Ministry of National Defence (MfNV) which oversaw the military. The _Grenztruppen_ became the fourth service branch of the [National People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Army "National People's Army") (NVA), the armed forces of the GDR. In 1973 they were separated and became directly subordinate to the MfNV, on grounds of not to be counted in MBFR. While wearing standard NVA uniforms, the _Grenztruppen_ had their own dark green arm-of-service colour, and their service and dress uniforms bore a green cuff title with white lettering "_Grenztruppen der DDR_" on the left arm. The vast majority of _Grenztruppen_ efforts were directed along the GDR's western borders with West Germany and West Berlin, with only about 600 members assigned to guard the GDR's borders with [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Poland "People's Republic of Poland") and Czechoslovakia. This continued until the 1980s when the rise of the Solidarity trade union in Poland saw the GDR considerably toughen the _Grenztruppen_'s presence along their border.
On 1 July 1990, the GDR's border control regime along the borders with West Germany and West Berlin was ended. In September 1990, shortly before the reunification of Germany, the _Grenztruppen_ were disbanded; its border patrol duties along united Germany's eastern frontiers were assumed by the _Bundesgrenzschutz_ (Federal Border Guard – later the _Bundespolizei_ or Federal Police).

## Pass and control units
[edit]
West German border personnel, civilians and an East German border guard on opposite sides of the border line at Herrnburg near Lübeck
For most visitors to East Berlin and the GDR, including persons who utilized the land transit routes (road and rail) between West Germany and West Berlin, their exposure to the _Grenztruppen der DDR_ consisted of dealing with the members of the Pass and Control Units (_Paß- und Kontrolleinheiten_, PKE) who processed travelers passing through the GDR's _Grenzübergangsstellen_ (border crossing points). Although they wore _Grenztruppen_ uniforms, the members of the PKE were in fact members of the 6th Main Department _(Hauptabteilung VI)_ of the _Stasi_.

## Organizational structure
[edit]
The headquarters of the _Grenztruppen der DDR_ was located at Bestensee-Pätz (a small village southeast of Berlin in the present-day state of Brandenburg), near Königs Wusterhausen.
The **_Grenzkommando Nord_** (GKN) [Border Command North], with headquarters at Stendal (in the present-day state of Saxony-Anhalt) was responsible for the northern sector of the East German border. The GKN consisted of five frontier troops regiments, two training regiments, a helicopter flight and some smaller support units. The _Grenzregiment 25 "Neithardt von Gneisenau"_ was disbanded in August 1983 and its units dispersed among the other border regiments of the command.
The **_Grenzkommando Süd_** (GKS) [Border Command South], with headquarters at Erfurt, guarded the southern border sector. The organizational structure of the GKS was similar to that of the GKN, with six frontier troops regiments, two training regiments, a helicopter flight and some smaller support units.

## After the Wall: The End of the Grenztruppen
The border troops did not survive the state they had defended. On 21 September 1990, ten days before German reunification, Defence Minister Rainer Eppelmann signed _Befehl_ 49/90, formally dissolving the _Grenztruppen der DDR_. Responsibility for the border passed to the _Bundesgrenzschutz_ (Federal Border Guard). Some former border soldiers were absorbed into the new structures; many were dismissed.
The border itself took years to remove. Under Bundeswehr direction, teams, some of them former border troops who knew the installations better than anyone, cleared the mines, dismantled the fences and watchtowers, tore up the patrol roads, and filled in the anti-vehicle ditches. The work continued until 1994. Today the death strip has become the _Berliner Mauerweg_, a 160-kilometre walking and cycling path that traces the entire circuit of the former Wall through the city. Where guards once patrolled with orders to kill, joggers and cyclists pass without a thought.

## The Watchtowers You Can Visit Today
Five watchtowers from the Berlin Wall fortifications survive in and around the city. Each has a different character, and together they give a physical sense of what the border looked like from the inside: the cramped observation rooms, the narrow stairs, the view across the death strip that the guards saw every shift.
The Grenzturm Nieder Neuendorf, a preserved command tower on the Havel, now a museum documenting the daily reality of the border service
The Gedenkstätte Günter Litfin in the Kieler Eck command tower near Berlin Hauptbahnhof is the most personal of the five. It was established and run for years by Jürgen Litfin, the brother of Günter Litfin, the first person shot dead at the Berlin Wall on 24 August 1961. The tower preserves the observation room and tells both Günter’s story and the broader history of the border fortifications at this stretch of the Spree.
The Führungsstelle Schlesischer Busch stands in Kreuzberg, on the edge of the former death strip near the Landwehr Canal. This was a command post rather than a simple observation tower, coordinating patrols across the sector. It now hosts a small exhibition on the border regime and temporary art shows.
The Wachturm Erna-Berger-Straße, just south of Potsdamer Platz, is a round observation tower of the BT-11 type that was standard along the Berlin Wall. Surrounded today by government buildings and new construction, it is a startling survivor — a piece of the fortified border standing in the middle of the reunified capital.
Further out, the Grenzturm Nieder Neuendorf sits on the bank of the Havel river northwest of Berlin. This is the most complete of the five: a full command tower with a well-preserved interior, now a museum that documents the daily reality of the border service: shift rosters, observation logs, the view the guards actually had. It is the closest thing to standing inside the system.
The Bergfelde Watchtower, in Brandenburg just beyond the Berlin city line, marks the outer ring of the fortifications. It stands at the edge of open fields where the border ran through farmland rather than city streets, a reminder that the Wall was only the urban face of a much longer frontier.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Did the border guards really have a shoot-to-kill order?
Yes. The _Schießbefehl_ was not a single document but a chain of written orders and oral instructions from 1961 to 1989, each authorizing lethal force against border crossers. Guards were trained to hit with the first shot, rewarded for killing, and punished for failing to fire. The order was secretly lifted on 3 April 1989, seven weeks after the last fatal shooting. See the full timeline above.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many people did the border guards kill?
At least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall between 1961 and 1989, the majority shot by border guards. On the whole inner-German border (from the Baltic coast to the Czech frontier) the total is higher. Eight border guards themselves were also killed on duty at the Berlin Wall.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many border guards escaped to the West?
About 2,500 border troops successfully defected over the life of the Wall, out of roughly 7,000 who attempted it. The most famous was Conrad Schumann, who jumped over the barbed wire on Bernauer Straße on 15 August 1961. Around 5,500 who tried and failed were caught and imprisoned.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Were the border guards punished after reunification?
Yes. In the _Mauerschuetzenprozesse_ (border-shooter trials) that ran through the 1990s, Berlin courts convicted 132 people: 80 guards, 42 military commanders, and 10 SED political leaders including Egon Krenz. The European Court of Human Rights upheld the convictions in 2001, ruling that the law of the GDR could not shield those who killed unarmed people trying to leave the country.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### Can you visit a Berlin Wall watchtower today?
Yes. Five watchtowers survive in and around Berlin, all marked on the interactive map. The Grenzturm Nieder Neuendorf has the most complete museum interior, while the Gedenkstätte Günter Litfin near Hauptbahnhof is the most central. See the watchtowers section above for all five.

## Frequently Asked Questions
### How many Berlin Wall watchtowers are left?
Five survive: the Gedenkstätte Günter Litfin (Kieler Eck), the Führungsstelle Schlesischer Busch, the Wachturm Erna-Berger-Straße, the Grenzturm Nieder Neuendorf, and the Bergfelde Watchtower. At the Wall’s peak, there were more than 300 watchtowers along the border around West Berlin alone.
